differential_diagnosis: AVRT (AV reentrant tachycardia) - less likely without delta waves on prior ECG

osces.candidate_instructions: 42-year-old woman presents to ED with 3-hour history of sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. She returned from a 14-hour flight from London 2 days ago. She takes the oral contraceptive pill and is a smoker. Vitals: BP 110/70, HR 115, RR 24, SpO2 92% room air, afebrile. Please assess and manage this patient.
osces.actor_instructions: You are a 42-year-old marketing manager who just returned from a business trip to London 2 days ago (14-hour flight). You developed sudden sharp right-sided chest pain 3 hours ago while at work, along with shortness of breath. The pain is worse when you take a deep breath. You feel anxious and have been coughing occasionally. You smoke 15 cigarettes daily for 20 years and take Microgynon 30 (combined OCP). You had a similar but milder episode yesterday but thought it was just tiredness from travel. You're worried something serious is wrong. You have no family history of clots but your mother had varicose veins.
osces.examiner_instructions: Observe the candidate's systematic approach to suspected pulmonary embolism. Key areas: recognizes clinical features suggestive of PE, interprets ECG findings (sinus tachycardia, possible S1Q3T3 pattern), calculates Wells score, initiates appropriate anticoagulation, orders CT pulmonary angiogram. Look for understanding of risk factors (recent long-haul flight, OCP, smoking) and knowledge of PE management protocols including NOAC vs LMWH options.

introduction_assessment.criteria: Professional introduction, recognizes potential emergency, systematic approach

focused_history.criteria: Pain characteristics (pleuritic), timing, recent travel, risk factors (OCP, smoking), previous episodes

examination.criteria: Focused cardiorespiratory exam, checks for DVT signs, oxygen saturation

ecg_interpretation.criteria: Identifies sinus tachycardia 115bpm, recognizes S1Q3T3 pattern (deep S in lead I, Q wave and T inversion in lead III), considers right heart strain

risk_stratification.criteria: Calculates Wells score (≥4 points: recent travel, tachycardia, no alternative diagnosis), considers PE as likely diagnosis

immediate_management.criteria: Oxygen therapy, IV access, initiates anticoagulation (rivaroxaban 15mg BD or enoxaparin 1.5mg/kg), orders urgent CT pulmonary angiogram

investigations.criteria: D-dimer (if Wells <4), ABG, FBC, UEC, coagulation, CXR, CT pulmonary angiogram, considers echocardiogram for right heart strain

ongoing_management.criteria: Discusses anticoagulation duration (minimum 3 months), OCP cessation, smoking cessation, follow-up arrangements

communication.criteria: Explains suspected diagnosis clearly, discusses treatment plan, addresses patient concerns about flying

sample_answer.history_summary: 42-year-old woman with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea 3 hours post-onset. Recent long-haul flight (London-Australia, 14 hours) 2 days ago. Risk factors: combined oral contraceptive pill (Microgynon 30), smoking 15/day for 20 years. Previous similar but milder episode yesterday. No family history of thromboembolism.
sample_answer.examination_findings: Anxious, mildly tachypneic. BP 110/70, HR 115 regular, RR 24, SpO2 92% room air, afebrile. JVP mildly elevated. Heart sounds: dual, no murmurs, loud P2. Chest: reduced air entry right base, no wheeze or crackles. Right calf slightly swollen compared to left, no tenderness or warmth. No peripheral cyanosis.
sample_answer.ecg_findings: Sinus tachycardia 115bpm. S1Q3T3 pattern present: deep S wave in lead I (4mm), Q wave in lead III (2mm), T wave inversion in lead III. Right axis deviation. No acute ST changes. Suggests acute right heart strain.
sample_answer.provisional_diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism with right heart strain
differential_diagnosis: Pneumothorax (but no sudden pleuritic pain pattern, normal CXR)
Pneumonia (but afebrile, no productive cough)
Musculoskeletal pain (but sudden onset, associated dyspnea)
Anxiety/panic attack (but objective findings of tachycardia, hypoxia)
wells_score_calculation: Clinical signs of DVT: 3 points (right calf swelling)
PE more likely than alternative diagnosis: 3 points
Total Wells Score: 9 points (high probability, >6 points = PE likely)
immediate_management: High-flow oxygen via Hudson mask (target SpO2 94-98%)
IV access x2, continuous ECG monitoring
Immediate anticoagulation: Rivaroxaban 15mg BD PO (preferred NOAC) PBS 11051X, OR Enoxaparin 1.5mg/kg SC BD if NOAC contraindicated
Urgent CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) - do not delay anticoagulation
D-dimer not required (Wells score >4, high clinical probability)
ABG: likely to show Type 1 respiratory failure, increased A-a gradient
FBC, UEC, LFTs, coagulation studies, troponin (exclude right heart strain)
CXR: may show wedge-shaped opacity, raised hemidiaphragm, or normal
Consider bedside echo if massive PE suspected (RV dilatation, McConnell's sign)
Analgesia: paracetamol 1g QID, avoid NSAIDs (bleeding risk with anticoagulation)
ongoing_management: Continue rivaroxaban 15mg BD for 21 days, then 20mg daily for minimum 3 months
If enoxaparin used: transition to warfarin (target INR 2.0-3.0) or NOAC after 5-7 days
Cease combined oral contraceptive pill immediately (major risk factor)
Alternative contraception: progesterone-only pill, Mirena IUD, barrier methods
Smoking cessation counseling + nicotine replacement therapy (PBS 4220K)
Graduated compression stockings 30-40mmHg for 2 years (prevent post-thrombotic syndrome)
Follow-up: GP in 1 week, respiratory/hematology clinic in 4-6 weeks
Repeat imaging at 3 months to assess clot resolution
Travel advice: avoid long flights >4 hours for 3 months, use compression stockings when flying
Thrombophilia screen if unprovoked PE or family history (protein C/S, antithrombin III, factor V Leiden)

learning_points: Wells score >4: high probability PE, start anticoagulation immediately before imaging
S1Q3T3 pattern: classic but only present in 20% of PE cases, indicates right heart strain
NOAC preferred over warfarin: rivaroxaban 15mg BD x21 days, then 20mg daily (PBS 11051X)
Combined OCP major risk factor: 3-6x increased VTE risk, must cease immediately
Recent long-haul flight: >4 hours increases VTE risk 2-4x, peaks at 1-2 weeks post-travel
CT pulmonary angiogram gold standard: 95% sensitivity, can detect subsegmental PE
Anticoagulation duration: minimum 3 months, consider extended if unprovoked or recurrent

osces.candidate_instructions: Mrs Margaret Chen, a 72-year-old retired teacher, presents to the cardiology clinic for evaluation of a heart murmur detected by her GP during a routine health check. She reports mild shortness of breath when climbing two flights of stairs and occasional fatigue. No chest pain or syncope. Conduct a focused cardiovascular assessment and advise on management.
osces.actor_instructions: You are Margaret Chen, a 72-year-old retired high school English teacher. You are generally healthy and active, walking your dog daily and doing tai chi twice weekly. Three weeks ago, your GP heard a heart murmur during your annual health check and referred you to cardiology. You've noticed mild shortness of breath when climbing the stairs to your second-floor bedroom, which you didn't have 6 months ago. You sometimes feel tired in the afternoons but thought this was normal aging. You have no chest pain, palpitations, dizziness or fainting. You take only amlodipine 5mg daily for mild hypertension diagnosed 3 years ago. Your mother had 'heart problems' and died at age 78. You're anxious about what the murmur means and whether you need surgery.
osces.examiner_instructions: Candidate should perform systematic cardiovascular examination, correctly identify aortic stenosis murmur characteristics, assess functional status, and discuss appropriate investigations and management. Look for recognition of moderate aortic stenosis requiring surveillance and symptom monitoring.

introduction_assessment.criteria: Professional introduction, explains examination, obtains consent

focused_history.criteria: Assesses exercise tolerance (NYHA class), chest pain, syncope, palpitations, family history, medications

inspection.criteria: General appearance, signs of heart failure, cyanosis, peripheral pulses

pulse_bp_assessment.criteria: Pulse character (slow-rising in AS), blood pressure, pulse pressure

cardiac_auscultation.criteria: Identifies systolic ejection murmur at aortic area, radiation to carotids, intensity grading (3/6), timing in systole

dynamic_maneuvers.criteria: Performs Valsalva or standing/squatting to differentiate murmur (AS decreases with preload reduction)

investigations.criteria: Discusses echocardiography (assess valve area, gradients), ECG, considers BNP if heart failure suspected

management_plan.criteria: Surveillance strategy, exercise advice, symptom monitoring, when to seek urgent review

communication.criteria: Explains findings clearly, addresses patient concerns, reassures appropriately

sample_answer.history_summary: 72-year-old woman with newly detected heart murmur, mild exertional dyspnea (NYHA Class II), and fatigue. No chest pain, syncope, or palpitations. Background hypertension on amlodipine. Family history of cardiac disease. Previously active with good exercise tolerance.
sample_answer.examination_findings: Alert, comfortable at rest, no cyanosis or pallor. Peripheral pulses present and equal. Carotid pulse slow-rising with delayed peak. BP 145/85, HR 72 regular. JVP not elevated. Cardiac inspection: no visible pulsations or deformity. Palpation: apex beat 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line, not displaced. No heaves or thrills. Auscultation: 3/6 harsh systolic ejection murmur loudest at right sternal edge 2nd intercostal space, radiating to both carotids. S2 present but soft A2 component. No diastolic murmur or gallop. Lung fields clear to auscultation. No peripheral edema.
sample_answer.provisional_diagnosis: Moderate aortic stenosis (based on murmur characteristics and mild symptoms)
differential_diagnosis: Aortic sclerosis (murmur without significant stenosis)
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (but murmur increases with Valsalva in HCM)
Pulmonary stenosis (but murmur location and radiation favor aortic)
investigations: Transthoracic echocardiography (assess aortic valve area, peak/mean gradients, left ventricular function) - MBS 55111
12-lead ECG (assess for left ventricular hypertrophy, conduction abnormalities)
BNP if heart failure suspected based on echo findings
Consider stress testing if asymptomatic severe AS to unmask symptoms
immediate_management: Reassure patient - murmur detected early, many people live normal lives with AS
Continue current medications (amlodipine appropriate for hypertension)
Avoid vigorous isometric exercise until echo assessment completed
Maintain regular light-moderate aerobic activity (walking, tai chi)
Advise on symptom monitoring: chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness/fainting
ongoing_management: Echo results will guide management strategy:
Mild AS (valve area >1.5cm², gradient <25mmHg): Echo surveillance every 3-5 years
Moderate AS (valve area 1.0-1.5cm², gradient 25-40mmHg): Echo every 1-2 years
Severe AS (valve area <1.0cm², gradient >40mmHg): Echo every 6 months, consider surgery if symptomatic
Blood pressure management: Target <140/90, ACE inhibitors safe in AS
Antibiotic prophylaxis NOT required for dental procedures (current guidelines)
Annual cardiology review, earlier if symptoms develop
Symptom education: Seek urgent medical attention for chest pain, syncope, or worsening dyspnea
Surgical referral if severe symptomatic AS (SAVR or TAVI depending on risk profile)

learning_points: Aortic stenosis murmur: Harsh systolic ejection murmur, right sternal edge, radiating to carotids
Pulse character in AS: Slow-rising (pulsus tardus) with delayed peak and reduced amplitude
AS severity grading: Valve area (mild >1.5, moderate 1.0-1.5, severe <1.0 cm²)
Dynamic maneuvers: AS murmur decreases with reduced preload (Valsalva, standing)
Surveillance intervals: Mild AS every 3-5 years, moderate every 1-2 years, severe every 6 months
Surgery indicated for: Severe symptomatic AS, severe AS with LVEF <50%, or undergoing other cardiac surgery
